Arlington Memorial Bridge runs across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery, one of six bridges connecting Virginia with the District of Columbia.
Arlington Memorial Bridge runs across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery, one of six bridges connecting Virginia with the District of Columbia.1
It was informally opened on January 16, 1932, when President Herbert Hoover drove across it.
Memorial Bridge connects in a direct line the Lincoln Memorial and the Civil War General Robert E. Lee’s home, Arlington House, on the hill overlooking Arlington National Cemetery, a deliberate connection designed to symbolize the re-joining of the north and the south after the Civil War. Just down the hill from Arlington House, and lying on that direct line, is JFK’s gravesite.
On the northeastern end of the Bridge, closest to Lincoln Memorial, are two large gilded bronze statues by Leo Friedlander named _The Arts of War_; the individual statues are _Sacrifice_ and _Valor_ and match two other statues at the entrance of Rock Creek Parkway known as the _Arts of Peace_. The statues were donated by the Government of Italy and dedicated on 26 September 1951, but the story of how they got there is interesting.
The original plans for these statues date back to 1928. They were originally designed to be carved from granite, but that became too expensive, so in 1931 plan was changed to a cheaper alternative: bronze. The plaster models were completed by 1938, but with war breaking out in Europe bronze became one of the many things rationed for the war effort. By the time the plaster models were brought out of storage at the end of the war, escalating prices had outpaced the project budget. So the Italians came to the rescue, proposing that the casting be done in Florence and Milan. The government of Italy would then donate the statues to the United States in appreciation for U.S. aid provided through the Marshall Plan. And having the Italians construct them solved another problem. The guilding process, dating back to Roman times, used a mix of gold and mercury; the mercury evaporates and leaves a fine layer of gold. But in the United States, working with mercury in that way was illegal due to health regulations. In Italy, however, it was still legal.2

The gilding doesn’t last forever. The statues were regilded in 1971, and the Park Service has since gone over them again, this time laying on 23.75-karat gold leaf rather than repeating the old mercury process. Alongside them, the two Arts of Peace groups at the Rock Creek Parkway entrance got the same treatment. If you’ve seen photos of the statues looking dull and dark, that’s what they looked like before the work; freshly gilded, they’re bright enough to pick out from the far end of the bridge.
Another interesting thing about the bridge is that, although it might not look like it, the center span was built as a drawbridge, designed to be raised to allow ships to pass through. It was last opened in 1961, and during the 2018-2020 rehabilitation the old bascule span was taken out and replaced with a fixed steel span, so the bridge no longer opens at all.3
The Arts of War statues aren’t the only sculpture on the bridge. At the Arlington end, four freestanding eagles designed by Carl Paul Jennewein sit atop the pylons flanking the approach, installed in 1938. Jennewein also did the bas-relief eagle medallions set into the bridge itself, 12-foot discs ringed by a wave border and flanked by fasces, which are easy to walk straight past unless you’re looking for them.
In the waters to the south of Memorial Bridge towards the 14th Street Bridge is where, in January 1982, an Air Florida flight crashed into the icy waters of the Potomac after taking off from nearby Reagan National Airport in bad, wintry weather, killing 78 people (74 on board and 4 motorists crossing the 14th Street Bridge).
From 2018 to 2020, Memorial Bridge underwent a $227 million rehabilitation that addressed serious structural issues that threatened the very viability of the bridge. It reopened fully to traffic, pedestrians, and cyclists in December 2020.

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
WASHINGTON — Dawn traffic crosses Arlington Memorial Bridge past the regilded Arts of War statues toward Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. The bridge carries Memorial Avenue over the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., and is administered by the National Park Service as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Italy cast and mercury-gilded the four bronze equestrian groups as a postwar gift, dedicated by President Harry S. Truman on Sept. 26, 1951. The columned building visible on the hillside is Arlington House, Robert E. Lee’s former home, sited to complete the bridge’s symbolic sightline between Lincoln and Lee. A 2018-2020 rehabilitation replaced the bridge’s obsolete bascule span with a fixed span, and a 2026 National Park Service project regilded the statues in 23.75-karat gold leaf for the nation’s 250th anniversary. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel
WASHINGTON — A jogger passes the gilded “Valor” and “Sacrifice” equestrian groups at the Washington entrance to Arlington Memorial Bridge in Washington, D.C., Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. The statues flank Memorial Avenue where it crosses the Potomac River toward Arlington National Cemetery, a span administered by the National Park Service as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Sculptor Leo Friedlander modeled the two bronze groups, known as The Arts of War, on granite pedestals designed by the architecture firm McKim, Mead and White. Italy cast and gilded the bronzes in 1949-50 as a postwar gift, and President Harry S. Truman dedicated them on Sept. 26, 1951. Each roughly 10-ton statue originally carried more than 100 pounds of 24-carat gold across the pair, applied by the mercury-gilding process. The National Park Service completed a $5.1 million restoration in 23.75-karat gold leaf on the Arts of War group in July 2026, timed to the nation’s 250th anniversary. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
WASHINGTON — Arlington Memorial Bridge spans the Potomac River toward Arlington House and Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. The National Park Service administers the Neoclassical crossing, which links the Lincoln Memorial to the cemetery’s hilltop entrance as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. McKim, Mead and White designed the bridge, built 1926-1932, aligning it on a sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House to symbolize post-Civil War reunification. Nine arches of white granite-faced concrete carry the roadway roughly 2,138 feet (652 m) between termini. Sculptor Carl Paul Jennewein designed the eagle medallions on the pylons visible along the balustrade. A 2018-2020 rehabilitation costing $227 million replaced the bridge’s obsolete drawbridge span with a fixed one, extending its projected service life by 75 years. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — The gilded bronze faces of the Sacrifice sculpture group catch morning light at Arlington Memorial Bridge, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. The equestrian statue stands at the bridge’s Washington terminus near the Lincoln Memorial, part of The Arts of War pair flanking Memorial Circle. Sculptor Leo Friedlander modeled the group, which was cast and gilded in Florence, Italy, in 1949-50 and unveiled by President Truman in 1951 as a Marshall Plan-era gift from Italy. The original mercury gilding was restored by brush electroplating in 1971-74, and the National Park Service applied fresh 23.75-karat gold leaf in 2026 under a $5.1 million contract with The Gilder’s Studio of Olney, Maryland. The companion Arts of Peace statues by James Earle Fraser stand nearby at the Rock Creek Parkway entrance. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
WASHINGTON — The Valor statue is silhouetted against a golden sky at the Washington entrance of Arlington Memorial Bridge, in Washington, D.C., in early October 2025. The 19-foot (5.8 m) gilded bronze equestrian group is one of two figures forming The Arts of War by sculptor Leo Friedlander, paired with the companion piece Sacrifice at the bridge’s Washington approach. Friedlander modeled the group by 1938, but wartime bronze shortages delayed casting until Italy produced it as a Marshall Plan-era gift between 1949 and 1950. President Truman unveiled the statue on Sept. 26, 1951, presented by Italian Prime Minister Alcide De Gasperi. The bridge behind it, completed in 1932 to a design by McKim, Mead and White, links the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery across the Potomac River. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — Pedestrians and cyclists cross Arlington Memorial Bridge in sunset glare, its granite balustrade catching the low light along the Potomac River, in Washington, D.C., in early October 2025. The Neoclassical bridge links the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. McKim, Mead and White designed the span, with William Mitchell Kendall as lead architect, and it was informally opened by President Hoover on Jan. 16, 1932. The bridge measures roughly 2,138 feet (652 m) between termini and carries nine arches faced in North Carolina granite. A 2018-2020 rehabilitation replaced its original bascule draw span with a fixed span, extending the structure’s service life by an estimated 75 years. The National Park Service manages the crossing as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
WASHINGTON — A carved granite eagle atop a pylon at the Arlington end of Arlington Memorial Bridge glows in late-afternoon light Monday, Oct. 6, 2025. The pylon stands at the bridge’s Virginia approach, near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial. Sculptor Carl Paul Jennewein designed the eagle as one of four freestanding figures crowning the bridge’s western pylons, part of a broader Neoclassical program that also includes his bas-relief eagle medallions within the bridge’s arches and bison keystones by Alexander Phimister Proctor. McKim, Mead and White designed the bridge, built 1926-1932 under chief engineer John L. Nagle. The National Park Service now maintains the span as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — The gilded bronze Sacrifice group, one of sculptor Leo Friedlander’s Arts of War statues, keeps watch over evening traffic at the Washington entrance to Arlington Memorial Bridge. Cast and gilded in Florence, Italy, as a postwar gift from the Italian government, the equestrian group was unveiled by President Harry Truman on September 26, 1951, alongside its companion Valor and James Earle Fraser’s Arts of Peace. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — Predawn traffic streams across Arlington Memorial Bridge past its gilded bronze equestrian statues, with Arlington House and Arlington National Cemetery visible on the Virginia hillside beyond. The Arts of War and Arts of Peace groups flanking the bridge’s Washington end were cast and gilded in Italy and unveiled in 1951; the bridge itself, completed in 1932, spans about 2,138 feet (652 m) between the Lincoln Memorial and the cemetery’s ceremonial entrance. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
ARLINGTON, Virginia — A carved granite eagle with wings outstretched guards the entrance road to Arlington National Cemetery against a clear blue sky. The cemetery, established in 1864 on the seized estate of Confederate General Robert E. Lee, occupies 639 acres (259 ha) on the Virginia bank of the Potomac and holds more than 400,000 interments as the nation’s preeminent military burial ground. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — Runners participate in the annual Cherry Blossom Ten Mile Run as they cross the Arlington Memorial Bridge, with the Lincoln Memorial standing prominently in the background. The bridge links the Lincoln Memorial with Arlington National Cemetery and serves as a key segment of the race route through the city’s monumental core, drawing thousands of participants each year during the National Cherry Blossom Festival. Completed in 1932 to a design by McKim, Mead and White, the low neoclassical structure — approximately 2,138 feet (652 m) long between termini and 90 feet (27 m) wide — was deliberately aligned on the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, encoding the reunification of North and South in its very geometry. The Lincoln Memorial, dedicated in 1922, honors Abraham Lincoln, the 16th President of the United States. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — Arlington Memorial Bridge stretches over a frozen, snow-covered stretch of the Potomac River during an unusually cold winter, linking Washington, D.C., to Arlington, Virginia. Built between 1926 and 1932 by McKim, Mead and White with chief engineer John L. Nagle, its nine granite arches span roughly 2,138 feet (652 m) on a sight line deliberately aligned between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
ARLINGTON, Virginia — A close view of Arlington Memorial Bridge’s granite paving reveals the fan-shaped cobblestone pattern set into the roadway surface near the Virginia approach. The bridge, faced entirely in bush-hammered white granite quarried in North Carolina and Georgia, was designed by McKim, Mead and White as the western terminus of the 1902 McMillan Plan’s monumental axis linking the Capitol, the Lincoln Memorial, and Arlington National Cemetery. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — Valor, Leo Friedlander’s gilded bronze equestrian group, rises above tree cover at the Washington end of Arlington Memorial Bridge, its granite pedestal ringed with 36 gilded stars for the states of the Union at the close of the Civil War. The statue and its companion group, Sacrifice, were cast in Italy and gifted by the Italian government, dedicated by President Truman in 1951. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial appear in silhouette at sunrise across the Potomac River, photographed from the Virginia shore. The bridge aligns on the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, a deliberate design by McKim, Mead and White encoding post-Civil War reunification. Its nine granite-faced arches were completed in 1932 after nearly a century of proposals and delays. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
ARLINGTON, Virginia — Arlington House, also known as the Robert E. Lee Memorial, crowns the hill above Arlington National Cemetery’s ceremonial entrance. Built between 1802 and 1818 by George Washington Parke Custis, the Greek Revival mansion became Robert E. Lee’s home after his 1831 marriage to Custis’s daughter. The 1901 McMillan Plan fixed this hilltop as the western terminus of Washington’s monumental core, aligned across the Potomac with the Lincoln Memorial. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Designing the statues
### Winning approval for the statue designs
By October 1933, the CFA had also resolved other aesthetic issues regarding the statues. In addition to approving the height of the statues (each would be 16 feet (4.9 m) tall), it set the height of the pedestals at 13 feet (4.0 m) and the height of the plinth beneath the statues at 1 foot (0.30 m).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1940CFA63-52) Granite from Mount Airy, North Carolina, would be used for the plinths and pedestals.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1940CFA63-52)

## Designing the statues
### Switch to bronze from granite
[edit]
James Earle Fraser (shown here in his studio) and his former student, Edward Minazolli, traveled to Italy to supervise the casting and gilding.
With little urgency, Fraser and Friedlander went ahead at a slow pace on their work.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-53) Partial funding for the granite statues was secured in 1935, but these monies were again impounded.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1940CFA63-52) The CFA asked Congress to approve funding for the statues in 1937,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-54) but this effort was unsuccessful. Additional efforts to win funding from Congress were made in 1938 and 1939, but also failed.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-GoldenHorses-55) Fraser and Friedlander completed work on their full-size models in 1939.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)

## Designing the statues
### Switch to bronze from granite
With the full-size plasters ready, the CFA made another push for funds in 1940. Money appeared to be available in the National Park Service budget, but bids for the granite and carving came in $70,000 too high. James Earle Fraser then suggested that the statues be cast in bronze or Benedict nickel[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1944CFA49-56) (an alloy of copper and nickel).[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-57) Friedlander and the CFA agreed with this suggestion, and in August 1941 both sculptors signed contracts to redesign their models for casting in bronze.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Rosenkranz9-34)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1944CFA49-56) For Friedlander, this meant removing the "web" supports beneath his horses and returning to his original design.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Rosenkranz9-34)
Lobbying Congress for money halted for a time while work proceeded on Friedlander's revisions. Money for the project became unavailable during World War II, and bronze was diverted to the war effort.

## Designing the statues
### Search for foundries
[edit]
On January 23, 1946, CFA member and sculptor Lee Lawrie visited the Friedlander workshop with an official of the National Park Service. They inspected the revised full-size model, and reported to the CFA on January 26 that it was satisfactory.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA49-58) By this time, however, the cost of casting in bronze had nearly doubled in the post-war period to more than $100,000 per statue.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Rosenkranz9-34) The National Capital Region of the National Park Service agreed to dismantle and store the Fraser and Friedlander models until such time as the prices for casting were more reasonable.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59) In the summer of 1947, Fraser surveyed foundries in Europe to see which might offer the least expensive casting. The single response indicated that it would cost $212,000 to cast both of his statues.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59) The Fraser and Friedlander statues were re-approved by the CFA in October 1947.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)

## Designing the statues
### Search for foundries
In January 1948, the National Park Service informed the CFA that about $1 million in authorized funds existed to complete Arlington Memorial Bridge.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-60) Fraser reported on his summer 1947 survey of foundry costs, and at the urging of the Park Service the CFA submitted legislation to Congress asking for an initial $185,000 appropriation to begin the casting process.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59) But the legislation did not pass in the first session of the 80th Congress.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-GoldenHorses-55)
At the CFA's meeting on September 13, 1948, the commission again discussed how to win an appropriation to complete the statue groups. The National Park made a survey American foundries, and told the CFA that few had been converted from war work back to art casting. Furthermore, only one foundry was large enough to handle the work, and it demanded an escalator clause in its contract. The park service expressed its opinion that an escalator clause would not be approved by federal budget officials. Members of Congress suggested, however, that a European nation be asked to cast the statues as part of the Marshall Plan. There was widespread agreement among CFA members and the sculptors that this should be pursued.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1959CFA52-61)

Arlington Memorial Bridge runs across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery, one of six bridges connecting Virginia with the District of Columbia.
Arlington Memorial Bridge runs across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery, one of six bridges connecting Virginia with the District of Columbia.1
It was informally opened on January 16, 1932, when President Herbert Hoover drove across it.
Memorial Bridge connects in a direct line the Lincoln Memorial and the Civil War General Robert E. Lee’s home, Arlington House, on the hill overlooking Arlington National Cemetery, a deliberate connection designed to symbolize the re-joining of the north and the south after the Civil War. Just down the hill from Arlington House, and lying on that direct line, is JFK’s gravesite.
On the northeastern end of the Bridge, closest to Lincoln Memorial, are two large gilded bronze statues by Leo Friedlander named _The Arts of War_; the individual statues are _Sacrifice_ and _Valor_ and match two other statues at the entrance of Rock Creek Parkway known as the _Arts of Peace_. The statues were donated by the Government of Italy and dedicated on 26 September 1951, but the story of how they got there is interesting.
The original plans for these statues date back to 1928. They were originally designed to be carved from granite, but that became too expensive, so in 1931 plan was changed to a cheaper alternative: bronze. The plaster models were completed by 1938, but with war breaking out in Europe bronze became one of the many things rationed for the war effort. By the time the plaster models were brought out of storage at the end of the war, escalating prices had outpaced the project budget. So the Italians came to the rescue, proposing that the casting be done in Florence and Milan. The government of Italy would then donate the statues to the United States in appreciation for U.S. aid provided through the Marshall Plan. And having the Italians construct them solved another problem. The guilding process, dating back to Roman times, used a mix of gold and mercury; the mercury evaporates and leaves a fine layer of gold. But in the United States, working with mercury in that way was illegal due to health regulations. In Italy, however, it was still legal.2
texts.1:
The gilding doesn’t last forever. The statues were regilded in 1971, and the Park Service has since gone over them again, this time laying on 23.75-karat gold leaf rather than repeating the old mercury process. Alongside them, the two Arts of Peace groups at the Rock Creek Parkway entrance got the same treatment. If you’ve seen photos of the statues looking dull and dark, that’s what they looked like before the work; freshly gilded, they’re bright enough to pick out from the far end of the bridge.
Another interesting thing about the bridge is that, although it might not look like it, the center span was built as a drawbridge, designed to be raised to allow ships to pass through. It was last opened in 1961, and during the 2018-2020 rehabilitation the old bascule span was taken out and replaced with a fixed steel span, so the bridge no longer opens at all.3
The Arts of War statues aren’t the only sculpture on the bridge. At the Arlington end, four freestanding eagles designed by Carl Paul Jennewein sit atop the pylons flanking the approach, installed in 1938. Jennewein also did the bas-relief eagle medallions set into the bridge itself, 12-foot discs ringed by a wave border and flanked by fasces, which are easy to walk straight past unless you’re looking for them.
In the waters to the south of Memorial Bridge towards the 14th Street Bridge is where, in January 1982, an Air Florida flight crashed into the icy waters of the Potomac after taking off from nearby Reagan National Airport in bad, wintry weather, killing 78 people (74 on board and 4 motorists crossing the 14th Street Bridge).
From 2018 to 2020, Memorial Bridge underwent a $227 million rehabilitation that addressed serious structural issues that threatened the very viability of the bridge. It reopened fully to traffic, pedestrians, and cyclists in December 2020.

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
WASHINGTON — Dawn traffic crosses Arlington Memorial Bridge past the regilded Arts of War statues toward Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. The bridge carries Memorial Avenue over the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., and is administered by the National Park Service as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Italy cast and mercury-gilded the four bronze equestrian groups as a postwar gift, dedicated by President Harry S. Truman on Sept. 26, 1951. The columned building visible on the hillside is Arlington House, Robert E. Lee’s former home, sited to complete the bridge’s symbolic sightline between Lincoln and Lee. A 2018-2020 rehabilitation replaced the bridge’s obsolete bascule span with a fixed span, and a 2026 National Park Service project regilded the statues in 23.75-karat gold leaf for the nation’s 250th anniversary. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel
WASHINGTON — A jogger passes the gilded “Valor” and “Sacrifice” equestrian groups at the Washington entrance to Arlington Memorial Bridge in Washington, D.C., Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. The statues flank Memorial Avenue where it crosses the Potomac River toward Arlington National Cemetery, a span administered by the National Park Service as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Sculptor Leo Friedlander modeled the two bronze groups, known as The Arts of War, on granite pedestals designed by the architecture firm McKim, Mead and White. Italy cast and gilded the bronzes in 1949-50 as a postwar gift, and President Harry S. Truman dedicated them on Sept. 26, 1951. Each roughly 10-ton statue originally carried more than 100 pounds of 24-carat gold across the pair, applied by the mercury-gilding process. The National Park Service completed a $5.1 million restoration in 23.75-karat gold leaf on the Arts of War group in July 2026, timed to the nation’s 250th anniversary. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
WASHINGTON — Arlington Memorial Bridge spans the Potomac River toward Arlington House and Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. The National Park Service administers the Neoclassical crossing, which links the Lincoln Memorial to the cemetery’s hilltop entrance as part of the George Washington Memorial Parkway. McKim, Mead and White designed the bridge, built 1926-1932, aligning it on a sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House to symbolize post-Civil War reunification. Nine arches of white granite-faced concrete carry the roadway roughly 2,138 feet (652 m) between termini. Sculptor Carl Paul Jennewein designed the eagle medallions on the pylons visible along the balustrade. A 2018-2020 rehabilitation costing $227 million replaced the bridge’s obsolete drawbridge span with a fixed one, extending its projected service life by 75 years. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — The gilded bronze faces of the Sacrifice sculpture group catch morning light at Arlington Memorial Bridge, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. The equestrian statue stands at the bridge’s Washington terminus near the Lincoln Memorial, part of The Arts of War pair flanking Memorial Circle. Sculptor Leo Friedlander modeled the group, which was cast and gilded in Florence, Italy, in 1949-50 and unveiled by President Truman in 1951 as a Marshall Plan-era gift from Italy. The original mercury gilding was restored by brush electroplating in 1971-74, and the National Park Service applied fresh 23.75-karat gold leaf in 2026 under a $5.1 million contract with The Gilder’s Studio of Olney, Maryland. The companion Arts of Peace statues by James Earle Fraser stand nearby at the Rock Creek Parkway entrance. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
WASHINGTON — The Valor statue is silhouetted against a golden sky at the Washington entrance of Arlington Memorial Bridge, in Washington, D.C., in early October 2025. The 19-foot (5.8 m) gilded bronze equestrian group is one of two figures forming The Arts of War by sculptor Leo Friedlander, paired with the companion piece Sacrifice at the bridge’s Washington approach. Friedlander modeled the group by 1938, but wartime bronze shortages delayed casting until Italy produced it as a Marshall Plan-era gift between 1949 and 1950. President Truman unveiled the statue on Sept. 26, 1951, presented by Italian Prime Minister Alcide De Gasperi. The bridge behind it, completed in 1932 to a design by McKim, Mead and White, links the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery across the Potomac River. McKim, Mead and White designed the span, with William Mitchell Kendall as lead architect, and it was informally opened by President Hoover on Jan. 16, 1932. ## Photos of Arlington Memorial Bridge
ARLINGTON, Virginia — A carved granite eagle with wings outstretched guards the entrance road to Arlington National Cemetery against a clear blue sky. The cemetery, established in 1864 on the seized estate of Confederate General Robert E. Lee, occupies 639 acres (259 ha) on the Virginia bank of the Potomac and holds more than 400,000 interments as the nation’s preeminent military burial ground. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**
WASHINGTON — Runners participate in the annual Cherry Blossom Ten Mile Run as they cross the Arlington Memorial Bridge, with the Lincoln Memorial standing prominently in the background. The bridge links the Lincoln Memorial with Arlington National Cemetery and serves as a key segment of the race route through the city’s monumental core, drawing thousands of participants each year during the National Cherry Blossom Festival. Completed in 1932 to a design by McKim, Mead and White, the low neoclassical structure — approximately 2,138 feet (652 m) long between termini and 90 feet (27 m) wide — was deliberately aligned on the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, encoding the reunification of North and South in its very geometry. The Lincoln Memorial, dedicated in 1922, honors Abraham Lincoln, the 16th President of the United States. Photo by David Coleman / Have Camera Will Travel**License this image at:AlamyDirectly**

ARLINGTON, Virginia — A close view of Arlington Memorial Bridge’s granite paving reveals the fan-shaped cobblestone pattern set into the roadway surface near the Virginia approach. The bridge, faced entirely in bush-hammered white granite quarried in North Carolina and Georgia, was designed by McKim, Mead and White as the western terminus of the 1902 McMillan Plan’s monumental axis linking the Capitol, the Lincoln Memorial, and Arlington National Cemetery. ARLINGTON, Virginia — Arlington House, also known as the Robert E. Lee Memorial, crowns the hill above Arlington National Cemetery’s ceremonial entrance. Built between 1802 and 1818 by George Washington Parke Custis, the Greek Revival mansion became Robert E. Lee’s home after his 1831 marriage to Custis’s daughter. The 1901 McMillan Plan fixed this hilltop as the western terminus of Washington’s monumental core, aligned across the Potomac with the Lincoln Memorial. ## Designing the statues
### Winning approval for the statue designs
By October 1933, the CFA had also resolved other aesthetic issues regarding the statues. In addition to approving the height of the statues (each would be 16 feet (4.9 m) tall), it set the height of the pedestals at 13 feet (4.0 m) and the height of the plinth beneath the statues at 1 foot (0.30 m).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1940CFA63-52) Granite from Mount Airy, North Carolina, would be used for the plinths and pedestals.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1940CFA63-52)

## Designing the statues
### Switch to bronze from granite
[edit]
James Earle Fraser (shown here in his studio) and his former student, Edward Minazolli, traveled to Italy to supervise the casting and gilding.
With little urgency, Fraser and Friedlander went ahead at a slow pace on their work.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-53) Partial funding for the granite statues was secured in 1935, but these monies were again impounded.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1940CFA63-52) The CFA asked Congress to approve funding for the statues in 1937,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-54) but this effort was unsuccessful. Additional efforts to win funding from Congress were made in 1938 and 1939, but also failed.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-GoldenHorses-55) Fraser and Friedlander completed work on their full-size models in 1939.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)
texts.19:
## Designing the statues
### Switch to bronze from granite
With the full-size plasters ready, the CFA made another push for funds in 1940. Money appeared to be available in the National Park Service budget, but bids for the granite and carving came in $70,000 too high. James Earle Fraser then suggested that the statues be cast in bronze or Benedict nickel[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1944CFA49-56) (an alloy of copper and nickel).[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-57) Friedlander and the CFA agreed with this suggestion, and in August 1941 both sculptors signed contracts to redesign their models for casting in bronze.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Rosenkranz9-34)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1944CFA49-56) For Friedlander, this meant removing the "web" supports beneath his horses and returning to his original design.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Rosenkranz9-34)
Lobbying Congress for money halted for a time while work proceeded on Friedlander's revisions. Money for the project became unavailable during World War II, and bronze was diverted to the war effort.
texts.20:
## Designing the statues
### Search for foundries
[edit]
On January 23, 1946, CFA member and sculptor Lee Lawrie visited the Friedlander workshop with an official of the National Park Service. They inspected the revised full-size model, and reported to the CFA on January 26 that it was satisfactory.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA49-58) By this time, however, the cost of casting in bronze had nearly doubled in the post-war period to more than $100,000 per statue.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Rosenkranz9-34) The National Capital Region of the National Park Service agreed to dismantle and store the Fraser and Friedlander models until such time as the prices for casting were more reasonable.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59) In the summer of 1947, Fraser surveyed foundries in Europe to see which might offer the least expensive casting. The single response indicated that it would cost $212,000 to cast both of his statues.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59) The Fraser and Friedlander statues were re-approved by the CFA in October 1947.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-Freundlich140-30)
texts.21:
## Designing the statues
### Search for foundries
In January 1948, the National Park Service informed the CFA that about $1 million in authorized funds existed to complete Arlington Memorial Bridge.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-60) Fraser reported on his summer 1947 survey of foundry costs, and at the urging of the Park Service the CFA submitted legislation to Congress asking for an initial $185,000 appropriation to begin the casting process.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1948CFA51-59) But the legislation did not pass in the first session of the 80th Congress.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-GoldenHorses-55)
At the CFA's meeting on September 13, 1948, the commission again discussed how to win an appropriation to complete the statue groups. The National Park made a survey American foundries, and told the CFA that few had been converted from war work back to art casting. Furthermore, only one foundry was large enough to handle the work, and it demanded an escalator clause in its contract. The park service expressed its opinion that an escalator clause would not be approved by federal budget officials. Members of Congress suggested, however, that a European nation be asked to cast the statues as part of the Marshall Plan. There was widespread agreement among CFA members and the sculptors that this should be pursued.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_of_War_and_The_Arts_of_Peace#cite_note-1959CFA52-61)

## Ohio Unfiltered's Post
[August 27](https://www.facebook.com/ohio.unfiltered/posts/pfbid02naeH2Ag181Lh3wGyoudFvHhFCV661G4sLDKqcQmZudCxk5GJ3BFuKzWfoviCQMcJl?__cft__[0]=AZjIX7yfB0e5ijO-cS2Q-CYlstAhGMe7Rg1FoJvlU3O7jnP-n1GdPBUpG4bjNecaJ2OxuZ7YRkjKf9kKEhIpm3S-vHG2js63_qwi9ykTgXP95MIiCunLPUsN8pp5vutd2hT-AVP1Eot3ZxdSq2yYBsFNicneT8byF1EP&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
There are eight enormous stone figures standing over a Cleveland bridge, and for about ninety years almost nobody outside the city knew what they were called.
The Guardians of Traffic were carved into the pylons of the Hope Memorial Bridge when it opened in 1932. Each one rises roughly forty three feet, faces the roadway, and holds a different vehicle in its hands, a covered wagon, a stagecoach, an early automobile, a truck, laid out as a progression of how people and freight moved. They were designed as a tribute to transportation itself and cut from Berea sandstone quarried nearby. The bridge is named for the family of Bob Hope, whose father worked as a stonecutter in Cleveland.
For most of the twentieth century they were simply part of the drive, the sort of monumental thing you stop registering somewhere around the hundredth crossing. Then in 2022 Cleveland's baseball team took the Guardians name, and suddenly eight Art Deco figures that had been standing quietly since Hoover was president were on national television.
Had you noticed the Guardians before the team took the name, or did you drive past them for years without looking up?

The **Hope Memorial Bridge** (also known as the **Lorain–Carnegie Bridge**) is a 4,490-foot-long (1,370 m)art decotruss bridge crossing the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland, Ohio. The bridge connects Lorain Avenue on Cleveland's west side and Carnegie Avenue on the east side, terminating just short of Progressive Field.
Four pairs of statues designed by sculptor Henry Hering and architect Frank Walker, officially named the _**Guardians of Traffic**_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-3) are sculpted onto opposite-facing ends of two pairs of pylons, a pair at each end of the viaduct. They symbolize progress in transportation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-4) Each Guardian holds a different vehicle in its hands: a hay wagon, a covered wagon, a stagecoach, and a 1930s-era automobile, as well as four types of motorized trucks used for construction.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-5) The statues are composed of Berea Sandstone and were carved in Cleveland's Little Italy neighborhood.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-7)
One of the eight _Guardians of Traffic_
A bond issue to pay for the bridge was passed in 1921, but construction was delayed for years due to squabbles over how the money would be spent. The bridge was completed in 1932 at a cost of $4.75 million ($112,090,000 with inflation[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-inflation-US-8)). It stands 93 feet (28 meters) above the river's waterline in order to allow shipping to pass unobstructed. A second, lower deck designed to carry truck and commercial traffic was never put into service.

The bridge had originally been planned to go through the location of the Erie Street Cemetery on East 9th Street.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-9)
The bridge was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on October 8, 1976, after a controversy in which Cuyahoga County engineer Albert S. Porter threatened to remove the historic pylons to widen the span, stating, "Those columns are monstrosities and should be torn down and forgotten. There is nothing particularly historic about any one of them. We're not running a May Show here."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-10)
The bridge was renovated in the early 1980s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-11)
On September 1, 1983, the Lorain–Carnegie bridge was officially renamed the "Hope Memorial Bridge". Press reports vary regarding whom the name honors: William Henry "Harry" Hope, a local stonemason who helped build the _Guardians of Traffic_ sculptures and the father of comedian and former Cleveland resident Bob Hope;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-13) Bob Hope himself;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-14) the entire Hope family;[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-17) or Harry Hope along with the other workers who helped erect the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-18)

On December 10, 2012, officials opened a 14.5-foot-wide (4.4 m) multi-use path on the north side of the bridge, part of a project which also added lighting to the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-19)
The inaugural Guardian Mile road race was run across the bridge on August 11, 2018. The elite field boasts multiple Olympians and $14,000 up for grabs in prize money, as well as races for runners of all ages and levels.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-20)
East end of bridge in relation to Progressive Field
On November 19, 2021, the Cleveland Indians of Major League Baseball changed their name to the Cleveland Guardians; the choice was inspired by the _Guardians of Traffic_, which neighbor Progressive Field, the team's home ballpark.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-21)

# Ohio Unfiltered - 🗿 There are eight enormous stone figures... | Facebook
## Ohio Unfiltered's Post
[August 27](https://www.facebook.com/ohio.unfiltered/posts/pfbid02naeH2Ag181Lh3wGyoudFvHhFCV661G4sLDKqcQmZudCxk5GJ3BFuKzWfoviCQMcJl?__cft__[0]=AZjIX7yfB0e5ijO-cS2Q-CYlstAhGMe7Rg1FoJvlU3O7jnP-n1GdPBUpG4bjNecaJ2OxuZ7YRkjKf9kKEhIpm3S-vHG2js63_qwi9ykTgXP95MIiCunLPUsN8pp5vutd2hT-AVP1Eot3ZxdSq2yYBsFNicneT8byF1EP&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
There are eight enormous stone figures standing over a Cleveland bridge, and for about ninety years almost nobody outside the city knew what they were called.
The Guardians of Traffic were carved into the pylons of the Hope Memorial Bridge when it opened in 1932. Each one rises roughly forty three feet, faces the roadway, and holds a different vehicle in its hands, a covered wagon, a stagecoach, an early automobile, a truck, laid out as a progression of how people and freight moved. They were designed as a tribute to transportation itself and cut from Berea sandstone quarried nearby. The bridge is named for the family of Bob Hope, whose father worked as a stonecutter in Cleveland.
For most of the twentieth century they were simply part of the drive, the sort of monumental thing you stop registering somewhere around the hundredth crossing. Then in 2022 Cleveland's baseball team took the Guardians name, and suddenly eight Art Deco figures that had been standing quietly since Hoover was president were on national television.
Had you noticed the Guardians before the team took the name, or did you drive past them for years without looking up?

The **Hope Memorial Bridge** (also known as the **Lorain–Carnegie Bridge**) is a 4,490-foot-long (1,370 m)art decotruss bridge crossing the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland, Ohio. The bridge connects Lorain Avenue on Cleveland's west side and Carnegie Avenue on the east side, terminating just short of Progressive Field.
Four pairs of statues designed by sculptor Henry Hering and architect Frank Walker, officially named the _**Guardians of Traffic**_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-3) are sculpted onto opposite-facing ends of two pairs of pylons, a pair at each end of the viaduct. They symbolize progress in transportation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-4) Each Guardian holds a different vehicle in its hands: a hay wagon, a covered wagon, a stagecoach, and a 1930s-era automobile, as well as four types of motorized trucks used for construction.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-5) The statues are composed of Berea Sandstone and were carved in Cleveland's Little Italy neighborhood.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-7)
One of the eight _Guardians of Traffic_
A bond issue to pay for the bridge was passed in 1921, but construction was delayed for years due to squabbles over how the money would be spent. The bridge was completed in 1932 at a cost of $4.75 million ($112,090,000 with inflation[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-inflation-US-8)). It stands 93 feet (28 meters) above the river's waterline in order to allow shipping to pass unobstructed. A second, lower deck designed to carry truck and commercial traffic was never put into service.

The bridge had originally been planned to go through the location of the Erie Street Cemetery on East 9th Street.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-9)
The bridge was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on October 8, 1976, after a controversy in which Cuyahoga County engineer Albert S. Porter threatened to remove the historic pylons to widen the span, stating, "Those columns are monstrosities and should be torn down and forgotten. There is nothing particularly historic about any one of them. We're not running a May Show here."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-10)
The bridge was renovated in the early 1980s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-11)
On September 1, 1983, the Lorain–Carnegie bridge was officially renamed the "Hope Memorial Bridge". Press reports vary regarding whom the name honors: William Henry "Harry" Hope, a local stonemason who helped build the _Guardians of Traffic_ sculptures and the father of comedian and former Cleveland resident Bob Hope;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-13) Bob Hope himself;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-14) the entire Hope family;[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-17) or Harry Hope along with the other workers who helped erect the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-18)

On December 10, 2012, officials opened a 14.5-foot-wide (4.4 m) multi-use path on the north side of the bridge, part of a project which also added lighting to the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-19)
The inaugural Guardian Mile road race was run across the bridge on August 11, 2018. The elite field boasts multiple Olympians and $14,000 up for grabs in prize money, as well as races for runners of all ages and levels.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-20)
East end of bridge in relation to Progressive Field
On November 19, 2021, the Cleveland Indians of Major League Baseball changed their name to the Cleveland Guardians; the choice was inspired by the _Guardians of Traffic_, which neighbor Progressive Field, the team's home ballpark.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-21)

# BRIDGING A CONNECTION
The Hope Memorial Bridge stretches nearly a mile across the Cuyahoga River in downtown Cleveland, standing just outside of the ballpark. It first opened in 1932 and was originally known as the Lorain-Carnegie Bridge. Designed by engineers Wilbur J. Watson & Associates and Frank Walker, the bridge was curved at the lower edge of its trusses to give it an arched appearance. The major architectural feature, however, is four massive stone pylons of eight figures representing the Guardians of Traffic, which were designed by Walker and sculpted by Henry Hering. Each Guardian holds a different vehicle including a covered wagon, stagecoach and 1930s automobile.
In the early 1980s, the bridge was closed for repair and upon reopening, it was renamed the Hope Memorial Bridge in honor of Bob Hope’s father who was a Cleveland stonemason. Recently, the Guardians have come to symbolize the spirit of Cleveland – resilient, hard working and loyal.
While inspired by the iconic sculptures of the Hope Memorial Bridge, our Guardians name is a reflection of the traits we, as Clevelanders, take pride in the most—fierce loyalty, unwavering support, and a resolve to stand side by side through thick and thin. As a team, as an organization, as citizens of Cleveland, we hope to protect and preserve all that we love about this city.

# BRIDGING A CONNECTION
### Script Guardians
The Script Guardians wordmark is an evolution of our script wordmark of the last 75 years. It is directly inspired by the architecture of the Hope Memorial Bridge, and the sharp, crisp angles of the letters mimic the trusses of the bridge's underside.

# BRIDGING A CONNECTION
### Diamond C & Bridge Print
The new Diamond C stands tall – just as the Guardians of Traffic stand watch over our ballpark and city – and draws from the ascending diamond motifs at the top of each Guardian pylon.
Our Bridge Print alphabet is derived from the Diamond C and will be used as a supporting element on our home and away jerseys. The new font represents the unique characteristics of Cleveland with angular letters and numbers that mimic the architecture of the bridge and the Guardians of Traffic.

# BRIDGING A CONNECTION
### Guardians Fastball
The Guardians Fastball logo embodies what it means to be a Cleveland Guardian in its strong, yet simple design. It is inspired by both the helmets and wings of Hope Memorial Bridge’s Guardians statues that keep watch over the city.

# Port of San Diego Statues: Unconditional Surrender & Bob Hope
If you are in Downtown San Diego, there are a couple of amazing statues located right next to the USS Midway, which are fun to take pictures of and/or with. The first one is Unconditional Surrender by J. Seward Johnson, and it is a 25-foot tall statue of the famous image of a sailor kissing a nurse from WWII. It is well done and beautiful with the sunset or the USS Midway in the background. It also makes for a fun statue to copy with your significant other. According to the website, it is only on loan until August 2010, but I was there in October of 201, and it was still there,so go check it out if you get a chance.

The other statue that they had there was a 1.3 million dollar statue of Bob Hope entertaining the troops. The price seems a little excessive to me, but the statue was pretty cool. It had Bob Hope standing in the middle with many different soldiers cheering him on as they watch. What was also interesting was that there was a stereo playing audio from some of his times entertaining the troupes while we were there, which added to the experience.
On the far side, there are also some wall memorials dedicated to members of the armed forces that lost their lives, and all of this is perfectly situated with the USS Midway right behind it.

# BRIDGING A CONNECTION
The Hope Memorial Bridge stretches nearly a mile across the Cuyahoga River in downtown Cleveland, standing just outside of the ballpark. It first opened in 1932 and was originally known as the Lorain-Carnegie Bridge. Designed by engineers Wilbur J. Watson & Associates and Frank Walker, the bridge was curved at the lower edge of its trusses to give it an arched appearance. The major architectural feature, however, is four massive stone pylons of eight figures representing the Guardians of Traffic, which were designed by Walker and sculpted by Henry Hering. Each Guardian holds a different vehicle including a covered wagon, stagecoach and 1930s automobile.
In the early 1980s, the bridge was closed for repair and upon reopening, it was renamed the Hope Memorial Bridge in honor of Bob Hope’s father who was a Cleveland stonemason. Recently, the Guardians have come to symbolize the spirit of Cleveland – resilient, hard working and loyal.
While inspired by the iconic sculptures of the Hope Memorial Bridge, our Guardians name is a reflection of the traits we, as Clevelanders, take pride in the most—fierce loyalty, unwavering support, and a resolve to stand side by side through thick and thin. As a team, as an organization, as citizens of Cleveland, we hope to protect and preserve all that we love about this city.

The Script Guardians wordmark is an evolution of our script wordmark of the last 75 years. It is directly inspired by the architecture of the Hope Memorial Bridge, and the sharp, crisp angles of the letters mimic the trusses of the bridge's underside.

# BRIDGING A CONNECTION
### Diamond C & Bridge Print
The new Diamond C stands tall – just as the Guardians of Traffic stand watch over our ballpark and city – and draws from the ascending diamond motifs at the top of each Guardian pylon.
Our Bridge Print alphabet is derived from the Diamond C and will be used as a supporting element on our home and away jerseys. The new font represents the unique characteristics of Cleveland with angular letters and numbers that mimic the architecture of the bridge and the Guardians of Traffic.

texts.1:
The **Hope Memorial Bridge** (also known as the **Lorain–Carnegie Bridge**) is a 4,490-foot-long (1,370 m)art decotruss bridge crossing the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland, Ohio. The bridge connects Lorain Avenue on Cleveland's west side and Carnegie Avenue on the east side, terminating just short of Progressive Field.
Four pairs of statues designed by sculptor Henry Hering and architect Frank Walker, officially named the _**Guardians of Traffic**_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-3) are sculpted onto opposite-facing ends of two pairs of pylons, a pair at each end of the viaduct. They symbolize progress in transportation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-4) Each Guardian holds a different vehicle in its hands: a hay wagon, a covered wagon, a stagecoach, and a 1930s-era automobile, as well as four types of motorized trucks used for construction.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-5) The statues are composed of Berea Sandstone and were carved in Cleveland's Little Italy neighborhood.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-7)
One of the eight _Guardians of Traffic_
A bond issue to pay for the bridge was passed in 1921, but construction was delayed for years due to squabbles over how the money would be spent. The bridge was completed in 1932 at a cost of $4.75 million ($112,090,000 with inflation[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-inflation-US-8)). It stands 93 feet (28 meters) above the river's waterline in order to allow shipping to pass unobstructed. A second, lower deck designed to carry truck and commercial traffic was never put into service.
texts.2:
The bridge had originally been planned to go through the location of the Erie Street Cemetery on East 9th Street.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-9)
The bridge was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on October 8, 1976, after a controversy in which Cuyahoga County engineer Albert S. Porter threatened to remove the historic pylons to widen the span, stating, "Those columns are monstrosities and should be torn down and forgotten. There is nothing particularly historic about any one of them. We're not running a May Show here."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-10)
The bridge was renovated in the early 1980s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-11)
On September 1, 1983, the Lorain–Carnegie bridge was officially renamed the "Hope Memorial Bridge". Press reports vary regarding whom the name honors: William Henry "Harry" Hope, a local stonemason who helped build the _Guardians of Traffic_ sculptures and the father of comedian and former Cleveland resident Bob Hope;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-13) Bob Hope himself;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-14) the entire Hope family;[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-17) or Harry Hope along with the other workers who helped erect the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-18)
texts.3:
On December 10, 2012, officials opened a 14.5-foot-wide (4.4 m) multi-use path on the north side of the bridge, part of a project which also added lighting to the _Guardians of Traffic_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-19)
The inaugural Guardian Mile road race was run across the bridge on August 11, 2018. The elite field boasts multiple Olympians and $14,000 up for grabs in prize money, as well as races for runners of all ages and levels.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-20)
East end of bridge in relation to Progressive Field
On November 19, 2021, the Cleveland Indians of Major League Baseball changed their name to the Cleveland Guardians; the choice was inspired by the _Guardians of Traffic_, which neighbor Progressive Field, the team's home ballpark.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Memorial_Bridge#cite_note-21)

opened.information:
Source: https://www.roadsideamerica.com/story/21525
Title: A National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military, San Diego, California
Chunks: 0,1
Bob Hope statue entertains the troops' statues.
San Diego, California
"Unconditional Surrender" -- the giant statue of a World War II sailor kissing a nurse -- was the reason we were loitering along Harbor Drive in San Diego. We were impressed by the statue's gaudiness and scale, against the imposing backdrop of a real US Navy aircraft carrier (USS Midway), and the procession of tourist photo subjects willing to stand next to it and look up the nurse's skirt.
"I have a wonderful make-up crew. They're the same people restoring the Statue of Liberty."-- Bob Hope
But then, right next door...what's this? An elevated plaza with the sign: "A National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military." And what looks from a distance like a small crowd assembled around a man at an old time-y microphone.
The figure with the mic is a bronze likeness of Bob Hope, the legendary movie/TV comedian and entertainer, in his prime. Before his death in 2003 at age 100, Hope had performed in hundreds of USO events since 1941, entertaining US military audiences in far-flung theaters of conflict, from World War II to the Gulf War.
Like some morale-igniting secret weapon, Bob Hope was deployed for maximum laugh efficacy, and much loved by men and women in uniform. In 1997, President Clinton bestowed on Hope the rank of "Honorary Veteran."
On the plaza, there are 15 life-sized bronze statues, arranged as if attending a Bob Hope show. Each figure represents a serviceman from a different conflict. The scene is completely open, allowing visitors to wander between the figures, and pose with them in reverent or irreverent pull-my-finger positions, or join the frozen crowd to cheer on Bob Hope's one-liners.
Women in the service are represented, as are wounded vets, with a racial diversity that underscores Hope's broad appeal. One figure holds up a sign with stenciled, punch-through lettering: "Thanks for the Memories BOB."
The "National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military" cost $1.5 million, and was a combined effort of the port of San Diego, the Hope family, and Navy vets of World War II's Battle of Leyte Gulf. The plaza and sculpture were officially dedicated in July 8, 2009, with two of Bob Hope's children on hand.

The sister version of "Unconditional Surrender" has gotten some heat in Sarasota, FL, where alleged art aficionados would eject all maudlin, representational sculpture and replace it with obtuse blocks and headache-inducing curlicues.
Appreciative servicemen; "Unconditional Surrender" statue in the background.
While Sarasota's smoochers may be threatened by blockheads, the art war seems over in Navy-friendly San Diego. There are plenty of abstract sculptures elsewhere in town, but here at the port more and more happy-go-lucky military bronzes are appearing on parks and lawns. All the figures around the park are collectively promoted as part of the "Greatest Generation Collection."
Bob Hope was a funny guy, a quipster with a lonnnng career. Though his relevancy started to wane in those last few decades, no equivalent master comic of the military-industrial complex has emerged.
This sculpture of a never-ending joke told to an eternally amused military is a fitting tribute.

**National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military**
**San Diego, California**
**About the Sculptures:**The bronze figures are sculpted in military uniforms authentic to the various eras of Bob’s career from World War II through the Korean War, Vietnam War, Cold War, and the first Persian Gulf War.
World War II Paratrooper
The 101st division (the Screaming Eagles) was activated on 15 August 1942 at Camp Claiborne, Louisiana on 19 August 1942. During World War II, the Pathfinders of the 101st Airborne Division led the way on D-Day in the night drop prior to the invasion. On 2 August 1944, the division became part of the First Allied Airborne Army. As part of this formation it took part in Operation Market Garden in the Netherlands. During the Battle of the Bulge the 101st defended the vital road junction of Bastogne. Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe replied to the demand for surrender: “To the German Commander: NUTS! —The American Commander.” (Some are convinced that what he actually wrote was less polite.) The division held its ground. This figure is of a sergeant in the 101st Airborne paratroopers, (not a pathfinder), who participated in the Normandy invasion.
Korean War Infantryman
We have chosen the 45th infantry division for this figure of a private for several reasons relating to the desire to honor Native American veterans. It was formed from citizen soldiers in the Southwestern U.S. It had at least two Native American Medal of Honor winners in the Korean War. Its insignia is the Native American thunderbird, and it is known as the Thunderbird division. The insignia is a strong clue for the viewing public the soldier may be Native American. Native Americans volunteered for service in Korea in higher proportion than any other identifiable ethnic group.
Gulf War Soldier in Desert Storm

Forty thousand women were deployed in Operation Desert Storm. Many, including those in the 82nd Airborne, were in combat and 16 were killed. This marks a change in American military history were many mothers with young children serve in the armed forces. The Desert Storm Gulf War soldier is an African American 2nd Lieutenant in the 82nd Airborne. The cast on her right leg emphasizes her combat role, and also serves to honor all wounded veterans. She has a notebook on her lap in anticipation of receiving an autograph from Bob Hope.
Korean War Sailor
More than 265,000 navy personnel served in Korea during the war. The U.S. Navy eliminated the North Korean navy, prevented and destroyed enemy troop landings, performed on-land reconnaissance, carried out allied troop landings, evacuated over 100,000 allied troops at Hungnam, bombarded shore positions, and launched thousands of aerial sorties. The Korean War sailor is a Seaman 1st Class, who will be holding one of the handles of the Gulf War soldier’s wheelchair. He is in his dress blues.
World War II Fighter Pilot
The World War II fighter pilot is a captain in the Army Air Force, with the 332nd Fighter Group (originally the 99th Fighter Squadron)—the Redtails—within the 15th Air Force. This group is famous for two reasons: 1) it is the only fighter escort group to lose no bombers to enemy fighters, and 2) it was composed entirely of African Americans. The 332nd shot down 111 German fighters, including at least two Me-262 jets, and earned 150 Distinguished Flying Crosses. They were also known as the Tuskegee Airmen because they were trained at Tuskegee Army Air Field in Tuskegee, Alabama. In 1949, pilots from the 332nd Fighter Group took first place in the Air Force National Fighter Gunnery Meet at Las Vegas Air Force Base, Nevada.
Vietnam War Artilleryman

This soldier is a private in an artillery unit from the Vietnam War. He is holding a home-made sign which reads “Go Bob!” He is wearing a T-shirt with no insignia, with his dog tags outside his shirt. US artillery in Vietnam was organized under I Field Force, II Field Force and XXIV Corps Artillery, consisting of 44 battalions in total. These battalions played a significant role in supporting American and allied infantry.
Vietnam War Air Force Mechanic
The mechanic is a Hispanic technical sergeant in the Air Force in the Vietnam War, seated on a wooden ammo box. A little remembered episode is that the first Air Force mechanics in Vietnam were sent in support of the French for seven months in 1954, in a deployment that grew to nearly 500 men. Their base at Do Son was under frequent attack, and the Viet Minh captured 5 men.
World War II Marine Corps Sergeant
The sculpture is of a patient from the 44th Field Hospital, one of the largest fully equipped hospitals in the Philippines during World War II. The Medical Statistics Division of the Office of the Surgeon General has estimated that close to 15,000 men in the U.S. Army, including Army Air Forces, suffered amputations during the period from 1 January 1942 to 31 March 1946. The maximum census reported by these amputation centers for any one month was 9,240 in June 1945. The figure is depicted in his issue blue robe, freshly pinned with the Purple Heart. “Bedside presentations” of this award, which would typically entail a general entering a hospital with a box of Purple Hearts, pinning them on the pillows of wounded service members, and then departing with no official records kept of the visit or the award. Service members themselves could complicate the issue by leaving hospitals unofficially, returning to their units. In such cases, even if a service member had received actual wounds in combat, the award of the Purple Heart might never be recorded in official records.
Korean War Marine

This sculpture of a Korean War Marine is of an African-American Marine shown in the standard issue cold-weather uniform required by the harsh Korean winter. Holding a sign marked “Thanks for the Memory” he communicates the support and appreciation of U.S. troops for Bob Hope and his efforts with the USO. African-American servicemen distinguished themselves in combat during the ground battles with the North Korean army and in the air war over Korea. The Korean War is considered by many as the turning point in the acceptance of African-Americans as proven members of the U.S. military. Following the Korean War, the Army abolished the 300 segregated all-black units that had previously existed and integrated the more than 300,000 African-Americans into the previously all-white units.
World War II Navy Machinist Mate

This figure is a portrait of a Machinist Mate, Third Class Petty Officer (PO3) from the USS Lark. The subject is depicted from the year 1944 as he would have appeared while stationed at MiosWoendi “Windy Island” in the South Pacific. The sculpture represents a sailor who served during the Battle of Leyte Gulf, which was fought in the seas around the Philippines following the initial landings and return of U.S. forces to these islands in October 1944. Consisting of four major air-sea battles fought over several days, including Taffy 3’s famous action in the Battle off Samar on 25 October, the Battle of Leyte Gulf was the greatest naval battle in history. In a last and desperate gamble to halt the advance of allied forces in the Pacific, most of the remaining major units of the still-formidable Imperial Japanese Navy were sent forth into this battle. In the Sibuyan Sea, off Cape Engaño, in Surigao Strait and off the island of Samar, U.S. sailors and airmen met, repulsed and defeated the Japanese fleet in this the last great naval battle between opposing fleets in World War II. The figure is depicted standing on a box in dungarees that were modeled from original period clothing acquired from the family of a World War II veteran. Further refinement to the uniform was based on information provided through oral history given by Hal Tinker, retired US Navy. The figure is a Caucasian male of approximately 22 years of age. The age of the sailor is based on footage of members of the audience at the MiosWoendi performance by Bob Hope featured on The Best of Bob Hope: The Ultimate Collection, “Bob Goes to War”.
Coast Guard Squadron One

Bob Hope statue entertains the troops' statues.
San Diego, California
"Unconditional Surrender" -- the giant statue of a World War II sailor kissing a nurse -- was the reason we were loitering along Harbor Drive in San Diego. We were impressed by the statue's gaudiness and scale, against the imposing backdrop of a real US Navy aircraft carrier (USS Midway), and the procession of tourist photo subjects willing to stand next to it and look up the nurse's skirt.
"I have a wonderful make-up crew. They're the same people restoring the Statue of Liberty."-- Bob Hope
But then, right next door...what's this? An elevated plaza with the sign: "A National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military." And what looks from a distance like a small crowd assembled around a man at an old time-y microphone.
The figure with the mic is a bronze likeness of Bob Hope, the legendary movie/TV comedian and entertainer, in his prime. Before his death in 2003 at age 100, Hope had performed in hundreds of USO events since 1941, entertaining US military audiences in far-flung theaters of conflict, from World War II to the Gulf War.
Like some morale-igniting secret weapon, Bob Hope was deployed for maximum laugh efficacy, and much loved by men and women in uniform. In 1997, President Clinton bestowed on Hope the rank of "Honorary Veteran."
On the plaza, there are 15 life-sized bronze statues, arranged as if attending a Bob Hope show. Each figure represents a serviceman from a different conflict. The scene is completely open, allowing visitors to wander between the figures, and pose with them in reverent or irreverent pull-my-finger positions, or join the frozen crowd to cheer on Bob Hope's one-liners.
Women in the service are represented, as are wounded vets, with a racial diversity that underscores Hope's broad appeal. One figure holds up a sign with stenciled, punch-through lettering: "Thanks for the Memories BOB."
The "National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military" cost $1.5 million, and was a combined effort of the port of San Diego, the Hope family, and Navy vets of World War II's Battle of Leyte Gulf. The plaza and sculpture were officially dedicated in July 8, 2009, with two of Bob Hope's children on hand.
texts.1:
The sister version of "Unconditional Surrender" has gotten some heat in Sarasota, FL, where alleged art aficionados would eject all maudlin, representational sculpture and replace it with obtuse blocks and headache-inducing curlicues.
Appreciative servicemen; "Unconditional Surrender" statue in the background.
While Sarasota's smoochers may be threatened by blockheads, the art war seems over in Navy-friendly San Diego. There are plenty of abstract sculptures elsewhere in town, but here at the port more and more happy-go-lucky military bronzes are appearing on parks and lawns. All the figures around the park are collectively promoted as part of the "Greatest Generation Collection."
Bob Hope was a funny guy, a quipster with a lonnnng career. Though his relevancy started to wane in those last few decades, no equivalent master comic of the military-industrial complex has emerged.
This sculpture of a never-ending joke told to an eternally amused military is a fitting tribute.
